proxy_compatibility.description: Direct compatible_pairs remain evidence-backed source-of-truth pairs. Named gameplay groups may use complete within-group compatibility or explicit group links, avoiding hundreds of enumerated proxy pairs.

group_links.note: Narrow gameplay proxy for large rocky exhibits containing similarly managed ibex, sheep, goats and tahr. It assumes ample escape routes, visual barriers and separation of incompatible breeding males; it is not a blanket all-caprine rule.
Curated cold-steppe/highland proxy for Domestic Yak with large Asian equids and caprines. Hot-desert ungulates and the Dromedary Camel profile are deliberately excluded.

Large-paddock gameplay proxy for Wisent with robust temperate deer and Wild Boar. Requires extensive space and separation options; rutting bulls, calving females and boar piglets require active management.
Conservative cold-climate gameplay proxy for Reindeer with Musk Ox and selected North American mountain ungulates. It assumes a large paddock, compatible individuals and seasonal separation.

Curated savannah proxy extending Kirk's Dik-Dik's existing giraffe, bongo and small-mammal mixed-exhibit evidence. Because dik-diks are tiny, territorial browsers, this rule assumes dense thorny refuge zones inaccessible to larger hoofstock and excludes aggressive predators and large pigs.

Narrow extension of Plains Zebra's thirty established combinations to six further open-savannah antelope already represented in comparable large mixed paddocks. It assumes substantial space and avoids small forest antelope, camelids and additional pigs.

Curated Zoo Curator proxy extending repeated Guanaco, Vicuña and Alpaca mixed-exhibit patterns across the four closely related South American camelids. Partners are restricted to established open-ground South American species; Fallow Deer and Sulawesi Babirusa are not inherited despite isolated direct records. Collared Peccary requires space and separation options.

Curated large-paddock gameplay proxy for Dromedary Camel. It combines repeated safari-park camel/giraffe/rhinoceros practice with compatible hot-desert antelope, Somali Wild Ass and Common Ostrich. This rule assumes substantial space, retreat areas and managed feeding; it is not transferred to cold-adapted Bactrian Camel.

Curated gameplay proxy based on large open-range Asian savanna practice, including San Diego Zoo Safari Park's Bactrian camel landscape with Asian deer, blackbuck, nilgai and banteng. It does not imply that every camel or every Asian hoofstock species is interchangeable.

Gameplay proxy for semi-aquatic pond/river turtles occupying water/moat space around arboreal/island primates. Supported by modern mixed-exhibit examples including squirrel monkeys/sakis with Yellow-Spotted Amazon River Turtles and Omaha primate/turtle exhibits. Excludes snapping turtles and other high-risk/specialist aquatic turtles from this broad proxy.

Gameplay proxy grounded in repeated modern lemur+tortoise exhibits, especially Ring-Tailed Lemur with Radiated/African Spurred Tortoise. This is an extrapolation for Zoo Curator, not a claim that every real-life individual/species mix is automatically safe.

Strong Zoo Curator gameplay proxy based on repeated modern Amazon/tropical-house exhibits. Lincoln Park Zoo explicitly mixes Yellow-Spotted Amazon River Turtle with Hoffmann's Two-Toed Sloth, White-Faced Saki and Golden-Headed Lion Tamarin; Omaha reports the turtle with Common Squirrel Monkey and sakis; Budapest reports Hilaire's Side-Necked Turtle with tamandua and emperor/golden-headed lion tamarins.

Broad gameplay proxy for non-predatory pond/river turtles using the water/moat layer of large mammal/primate exhibits. Supported by repeated zoo practice and specific modern examples, but intentionally excludes snapping turtles, softshell turtles and specialist/predatory aquatic turtles from the pond_turtles group.

Broad Zoo Curator proxy supported by modern mixed wetland exhibits. Eurasian Spoonbill is housed with Chilean Flamingo at Dublin Zoo; Roseate Spoonbill with Caribbean/American Flamingo at Toledo Zoo; African Spoonbill with Greater Flamingo in the successful Odense Zoo African waterbird aviary.

Broad wetland-bird proxy. Odense Zoo successfully bred African Spoonbill and Pink-Backed Pelican together; other modern collections repeatedly hold spoonbills and pelicans in mixed wetland assemblages.

Broad wetland-bird proxy anchored by the successful Greater Flamingo + Pink-Backed Pelican Odense Zoo mixed aviary. Pelican predation on eggs/chicks can occur, so this represents viable exhibit cohabitation rather than zero-risk breeding compatibility.

Large-public-aquarium gameplay proxy. Modern public aquaria routinely maintain selected sharks and rays together in very large systems. Species selection and feeding remain important; freshwater rays and Tiger Shark are excluded from this broad rule.
Large-public-aquarium gameplay proxy for Green Sawfish with the curated shark roster. It represents professionally managed, very large multispecies systems; Tiger Shark remains excluded.
Large-public-aquarium gameplay proxy for Green Sawfish with marine rays. Freshwater stingrays are deliberately outside this rule.

Curated large-aquarium proxy for sea turtles with established public-aquarium sharks. Existing direct records already anchor Green, Hawksbill and Loggerhead turtles with Bonnethead Shark. Tiger Shark is excluded because its predation risk is not appropriate for blanket compatibility.
Curated large-aquarium proxy for marine sea turtles with marine rays in spacious public-aquarium systems. It does not include freshwater stingrays.

Zoo Curator gameplay proxy anchored by a published Parma Wallaby + Patagonian Mara compatibility study at Dudley Zoo. Apply to low-conflict open-ground macropods/maras; individual husbandry still matters.

Broad tropical-house proxy: agoutis repeatedly occupy the terrestrial layer below sloths and small/medium New World primates. Supported by white-faced saki husbandry reports and modern South American walkthrough exhibits.

Broad ground-vs-arboreal gameplay proxy anchored by Cleveland Metroparks Zoo's 2018 mix of Southern Three-Banded Armadillo with Linne's Two-Toed Sloth, Golden Lion Tamarin, Goeldi's Monkey and White-Faced Saki.

Directly supported by modern tropical-house records, including Hoffmann's Two-Toed Sloth with a Dasyprocta agouti at CREA (2024) and Linne's Two-Toed Sloth with Dasyprocta leporina in BioParque do Rio.
Supported by Cleveland Metroparks Zoo (Linne's Two-Toed Sloth + Southern Three-Banded Armadillo, 2018) and Chelyabinsk Zoo (Linne's Two-Toed Sloth + Six-Banded Armadillo, 2010).

Zoo Curator rule: modern Golden Lion Tamarin + two-toed sloth evidence extends to the full tamarins gameplay group. Smithsonian documents Golden Lion Tamarins and two-toed sloths as long-term exhibit mates; Cleveland Metroparks also documents Golden Lion Tamarin + Linne's Two-Toed Sloth.

Zoo Curator rule: modern Golden Lion Tamarin + armadillo evidence extends to the full tamarins gameplay group. Cleveland Metroparks Zoo documented Golden Lion Tamarin + Southern Three-Banded Armadillo in the same 2018 mixed exhibit.

Zoo Curator rule: Golden Lion Tamarin + agouti evidence extends to the full tamarins gameplay group. Jerusalem Biblical Zoo documented Golden Lion Tamarin + Dasyprocta leporina in 2007; Houston Zoo describes Golden Lion Tamarins sharing a mixed habitat with red-rumped agoutis.

Requested Zoo Curator gameplay proxy. Capuchins share broadly similar arboreal/omnivorous ecology and mixed-primate husbandry precedents. Tufted capuchins have especially strong mixed-species evidence. This does not claim that every capuchin species pair is routinely co-housed in real zoos; introductions, sex composition and escape/refuge design still matter.

Requested Zoo Curator gameplay proxy. Mixed macaque exhibits have real institutional precedent, including a long-running National Zoological Park association involving Barbary, lion-tailed and Sulawesi macaques. Because macaques can be socially assertive and closely related species may hybridize, this is a gameplay compatibility rule rather than a blanket real-world husbandry recommendation.

Six distinct Zoo Curator tamarins/marmosets already have direct modern red-footed-tortoise mixed-exhibit evidence. The remaining tamarin-group members inherit this low-conflict terrestrial-versus-arboreal gameplay compatibility.

Southern Three-Banded Armadillo is directly documented with Red-Footed Tortoise, while multiple other armadillos are independently documented with the same low-conflict tropical-house mammals. Zoo Curator extends this managed ground-layer pattern to the armadillo group.

Modern mixed-exhibit evidence supports Red-Footed Tortoise with both two-toed-sloth taxa represented by the Zoo Curator group; this explicit link also prevents spelling variants from fragmenting the rule.

Seven of eight cross-pairs are already directly documented at named institutions. The single inferred pair is Banded Mongoose + African Spurred Tortoise. Breeding animals still require refuge and monitoring.

A deliberately narrow South American open-grassland proxy supported by multiple modern rhea exhibits. It excludes predators, very small species and dense-forest specialists; individual rheas can still be assertive during breeding.

Gameplay extrapolation grounded in multiple actual zoo exhibits: Pond Slider with Cuvier's, Spectacled and Yacare Caimans; Cuvier's Dwarf Caiman with Arrau, Yellow-Spotted Amazon River, Geoffroy's Side-Necked and Neotropical Painted Wood Turtles; and Yacare Caiman with Mata-Mata. Intended for large adults, ample water/land space, refuges and managed feeding—not as zero-risk breeding advice.

Strong gameplay proxy. Five members already have direct Emu evidence in this dataset (Agile, Parma and Red-Necked Wallabies plus Red and Grey Kangaroos). The rule extends that repeated open-walkthrough pattern to Swamp Wallaby, Eastern Wallaroo, Dusky Pademelon and Yellow-Footed Rock Wallaby; breeding males and small macropods still require space, refuge and monitoring.

Cautious layer-based proxy. Koala + Swamp Wallaby is already a direct pair; Healesville's Koalas area also associates koalas with Parma Wallaby and a pademelon, while Kookaburra Animal Park documents a walkthrough zone containing koala, Red Kangaroo and Red-Necked Wallaby. This does not extend to every ground macropod or imply unrestricted access to koala feeding/rest trees.

Narrow gameplay proxy. Common Wombat + Swamp Wallaby is directly documented in the dataset; Budapest's Australian zone places Common Wombat and Red Kangaroo in the same small Australian complex, and field research records wallabies and kangaroos repeatedly using common-wombat burrow landscapes. Kept to four robust/common ground macropods rather than the full wallaby group because wombats are powerful, burrowing and often solitary.

Narrow New Guinea forest-layer proxy. Both Goodfellow's and Matschie's Tree-Kangaroos already have direct Dusky Pademelon evidence; Avilon Zoo also holds Matschie's Tree-Kangaroo alongside Dorcopsis records, supporting cautious extension to Brown Dorcopsis. Tree-kangaroos are not made compatible with one another, and the rule does not extend to Australian kangaroos or wallabies.

Requested Zoo Curator gameplay rule: the listed New World macaws, mainland Neotropical parrots and geographically eligible Amazons inherit one another's established external partners. Central American taxa are included when their native mainland range reaches modern sloth territory: White-Crowned Parrot, White-Fronted Amazon and Yellow-Naped Amazon qualify. Yellow-Headed Amazon is excluded from this profile because its only Honduran range is in the far northwest/lower Sula Valley, while Hoffmann's Two-Toed Sloth begins in eastern Honduras. Cuban, Yellow-Billed and Yucatan Amazons are excluded as island/Yucatan endemics without modern native sloth overlap; Red-Crowned and Lilac-Crowned Amazons are excluded as Mexico-only taxa. African Grey, Timneh, Senegal, Meyer's and Red-Fronted Parrots, Kea and Northern Kaka are also excluded. This is a gameplay extrapolation, not proof that every generated pair has been directly co-housed.

Designer-approved tropical-house proxy. The 40 eligible New World psittacines may share a sufficiently large, planted, structurally complex tropical house with the listed low-conflict terrestrial, aquatic-edge and small/medium arboreal South American mammals. This extends the existing sloth, Cotton-Top Tamarin, Goeldi's Monkey and Southern Three-Banded Armadillo anchors to all tamarins/marmosets, all four armadillos, all three agoutis, Lowland Paca, Capybara, Brazilian Porcupine, Southern Tamandua, maras, Plains Viscacha, squirrel monkeys, howlers, sakis, Red Titi, Grey-Handed Night Monkey and Brown-Throated Sloth. It represents managed exhibit viability, not unrestricted contact, breeding-season safety or identical husbandry needs.

Requested cautious gameplay rule for South American Coati and Kinkajou. Both are agile climbers and potential nest/food competitors, so this compatibility assumes a very large zoned tropical house, inaccessible bird nesting and feeding stations, vertical refuges and managed introductions. It is deliberately separate from the lower-risk mammal group and is not a blanket real-world safety claim.

Gameplay proxy based on large free-flight tropical-house practice. These fruit bats and flying foxes are Old World rather than South American, but occupy a comparable nocturnal aerial/canopy layer and have mixed-tropical-house precedent alongside parrots and small primates. Compatibility assumes substantial flight volume, separate roosting/feeding areas and monitoring.

Low-conflict forest-floor proxy for Red-Footed and Yellow-Footed Tortoises beneath free-flying Neotropical parrots. Arid and island giant tortoises are not generalized into this rule merely because they belong to the broader tortoise gameplay group.

Requested water-layer proxy for the established non-predatory pond-turtle group beneath free-flying parrots. It assumes separated dry basking/rest areas, adequate water quality and species-appropriate temperatures; snapping turtles, softshells and other predatory or specialist turtles remain excluded.

Adds the curated South American robust water-turtle group, including Arrau River Turtle, Mata-Mata, Geoffroy's Side-Necked Turtle and Neotropical Painted Wood Turtle, to the tropical-house bird profile. This is a habitat-layer rule; suitable water depth, feeding separation and haul-out areas remain necessary.

Conservative African small-antelope proxy. Aardvark has named-institution evidence with Kirk's Dik-Dik and multiple duikers; Bongo is already directly documented/curated with Kirk's Dik-Dik, Red Duiker and Yellow-Backed Duiker. This does NOT make all savannah/forest partners interchangeable.

Muntjacs and Tufted Deer share repeated mixed-exhibit patterns with Red Panda; Binturong is directly documented with Indian and Reeves' Muntjac and reported successfully with Tufted Deer in husbandry literature. Large-hoofstock partners are deliberately not propagated across this group.

Mouse-deer/chevrotains remain separate from the muntjac/Tufted Deer core. EAZA loris guidance reports successful Tragulus spp. with Nycticebus spp.; Grey Slender Loris direct pairs are retained and Pygmy Slow Loris is added through this narrow proxy.

Closely related Oryx managed in the same AZA aridland-antelope husbandry category; Zoo Curator rarity proxy shares established mixed-ungulate/bird partners, without making the two oryx automatically compatible with one another.

Cross-institutional husbandry research shows Southern and Nile lechwe repeatedly used in highly overlapping mixed-species assemblages; share established partners without making the two lechwe automatically compatible.
Conservative rarity proxy: shares established non-callitrichid partners only; does not make all tamarins mutually compatible.
Conservative rarity proxy: shares established non-callitrichid partners only; does not make all marmosets mutually compatible.
Linnaeus's and Hoffmann's two-toed sloths share established low-risk mixed-exhibit partners; large-predator and other-sloth edges are excluded from inheritance.
Conservative external-partner inheritance for Large Hairy, Six-Banded and Southern Three-Banded Armadillos. Nine-Banded Armadillo excluded; known/high-risk small-prey relationships blocked.

Restricted to Green and Violet Turaco: ZooLex documents both together in Rotterdam Congo Forest with the same mixed aviary community. Other turacos excluded because published work reports potentially severe inter-turaco aggression.

Flamingo-style Zoo Curator proxy for large Old World fruit bats/flying foxes. The five represented taxa are treated as an interchangeable aerial tropical-house guild because modern zoo evidence shows repeated cross-species fruit-bat housing (Indian Flying Fox + Egyptian Fruit Bat; Rodrigues Flying Fox + Egyptian Fruit Bat; and a reported Hagenbeck tropical-hall combination of Rodrigues, Egyptian and Large Flying Fox) and repeated mixed tropical-house use with terrestrial, aquatic and arboreal mammals, tortoises, reptiles and birds. Partner inheritance is deliberately restricted to low-conflict species already directly evidenced with at least one member of the guild, plus Kinkajou (Egyptian Fruit Bat at Poznan). This is a gameplay husbandry proxy, not a claim that geography matches or that every individual mix is risk-free.

Conservative flying-fox/free-flight-bird inheritance. Rodrigues Flying Fox has a named mixed rainforest exhibit at Central Park with Scarlet Ibis, Black-naped Fruit Dove, Nicobar Pigeon, Yellow-breasted Ground Dove, Victoria Crowned Pigeon, Sunbittern and Violet Turaco; Beauval documents/has reported Rodrigues with Von Der Decken's Hornbill and other birds. Indian Flying Foxes free-range through Sedgwick County Zoo's bird-dominated Tropics building and Topeka's tropical rainforest with free-roaming birds. Lyle's Flying Fox has also been observed mixed with a cockatiel at Castellar. This supports a cross-Pteropus aerial-layer proxy, but NOT blanket compatibility with every tropical bird, especially raptors, aggressive parrots, or small vulnerable species without a suitable spatially complex free-flight setting.

Conservative overhead-layer proxy for the five large fruit-bat/flying-fox taxa. Repeated independent zoo precedents show guild members above terrestrial or lower-canopy mammals: Indian/Egyptian/Rodrigues with Aardvark; Egyptian with Kinkajou; Egyptian and Rodrigues independently with Hippopotamus; Rodrigues with Sitatunga; Rodrigues with bettongs/woylies; Indian with Linnaeus's Two-Toed Sloth; Egyptian in Haus des Meeres tropical hall with Goeldi's Monkey and White-Faced Saki; and Lyle's Flying Fox directly with Belly-banded Squirrel and with Ground Cuscus + Brush-tailed Rat-kangaroo. This supports interchangeability for low-conflict vertical-niche mixes, not blanket compatibility with all arboreal mammals.

Conservative ground-layer inheritance for the large-fruit-bat guild. Modern/traceable records include Large Flying Fox with Red-Footed Tortoise at Aquario de Sao Paulo (2025); Rodrigues Flying Fox with Aldabra Giant Tortoise at Beauval; and a reported Columbus Asia Quest mix of Large Flying Fox with Aldabra, Radiated and Burmese mountain tortoises plus Malayan chevrotain. San Diego also mixed Rodrigues Flying Fox + Egyptian Fruit Bat + Aardvark + Tokay Gecko. This supports low-conflict terrestrial reptiles and tiny ungulates beneath the aerial bat layer, but does not justify blanket inheritance to porcupines, agoutis, tenrecs, armadillos, lemurs, or every tortoise species without a closer anchor.

Strong institutional anchor: the Zoological Society of London's archive describes Rainforest Life's main walk-through as jointly housing Rodrigues Flying Fox with two-toed sloths, Golden Lion Tamarins, Emperor Tamarins, Red Titi Monkeys, Red-faced Spider Monkeys, big hairy armadillos, Geoffrey's marmosets, Cotton-top Tamarins, Goeldi's marmosets and Southern Tamandua. Because independent records also show Egyptian fruit bats with Goeldi's/White-faced Saki, Indian flying fox with sloth, and Lyle's flying fox with arboreal/ground small mammals, Zoo Curator treats these low-conflict rainforest mammals as an interchangeable partner layer for the large-fruit-bat guild. This is a husbandry/gameplay proxy, not a claim of biogeographic authenticity.

Group-level transfer based on ZSL Rainforest Life directly housing Rodrigues Flying Fox with Golden Lion, Emperor and Cotton-top Tamarins plus Goeldi's marmoset, while other fruit-bat tropical-house records also anchor Goeldi's. Zoo Curator therefore allows closely comparable callitrichids already represented in its tamarin/marmoset compatibility logic to inherit the flying-fox aerial-layer relationship. This is proxy compatibility, not a claim that every listed callitrichid has a species-identical published bat record.

Cincinnati is a strong named record: Aardvark + Mongoose Lemur + Indian Flying Fox + Egyptian Fruit Bat. This establishes Mongoose Lemur with two members of the fruit-bat guild simultaneously. It is NOT expanded to the general lemur group yet.

ZSL directly anchors Red Titi with Rodrigues Flying Fox; Haus des Meeres independently reports Egyptian Fruit Bat with White-Faced Saki. With both sides of the titi/saki gameplay cluster independently anchored to fruit bats, the existing Zoo Curator titi/saki grouping is inherited conservatively.
ZSL directly anchors Red-Faced Spider Monkey with Rodrigues Flying Fox. Propagation is restricted to the game's existing spider-monkey equivalence group rather than all atelids or all monkeys.

ZSL directly anchors Large Hairy Armadillo with Rodrigues Flying Fox. ZooRope independently records Egyptian Fruit Bat + Large Hairy Armadillo + Kinkajou at Omaha, giving a second fruit-bat/armadillo anchor. This is enough for Zoo Curator's established armadillo gameplay group, but not for unrelated digging mammals.

ZSL anchors two-toed sloth with Rodrigues Flying Fox and Topeka independently mixes Indian Flying Fox with Linnaeus's Two-Toed Sloth. This repeated cross-bat evidence supports the game's existing two-toed-sloth group.
ZSL directly anchors Southern Tamandua with Rodrigues Flying Fox. This is restricted to tamanduas; it is not generalized to giant anteaters.

Budapest directly mixes Lyle's Flying Fox with Brush-tailed rat-kangaroo and Ground Cuscus; a 2024 Gan Garoo record independently mixes Grey-headed Flying Fox with Brush-tailed rat-kangaroo; Olomouc is reported with Rodrigues Flying Fox plus bettongs/woylies/rufous rat-kangaroos. This supports close small-marsupial ground-layer transfer, not all marsupials.

Tokyo Zoo's official video archive explicitly records Orii Flying Fox with Javan lesser mouse deer (2005 and 2008), while Singapore's Fragile Forest independently mixes Malayan Flying Fox with Lesser Mouse-deer. This supports the game's Javan/Lesser mouse-deer layer but not every chevrotain species.

Restricted tropical-squirrel inheritance. Singapore Zoo's current official Fragile Forest page places Malayan flying foxes in the biodome canopy/understorey community that also includes Prevost's squirrel, while Pairi Daiza independently documents Lyle's Flying Fox with Belly-banded Squirrel. A historical named Brookfield/Lincoln Park mix also combines Island Flying Fox and Lesser Dog-faced Fruit Bat with Black Giant Squirrel. Multiple fruit-bat and squirrel taxa therefore support the same vertical-niche pattern. This does not extend to temperate/ground squirrels or tree shrews.
